Europol Disrupts AudiA6 Crypto Laundering Service Used by Ransomware Gangs

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Authorities in Europe have disrupted AudiA6, a cryptocurrency laundering service used by ransomware gangs and cybercriminal networks. Europol, in a statement issued Thursday, said the dismantling of AudiA6 cut off a "key financial pipeline used to wash hundreds of millions in illicit profits." The service is estimated to have been used to launder more than €336 million (~$389 million) since the

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound or outbound email involving AudiA6 mule-recruitment domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/network contact with AudiA6 money-mule registration domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DNS/network contact with AudiA6 money-mule registration domains AICommand & Control High
Detects endpoints resolving or connecting to the 19 email-infrastructure domains Europol linked to the AudiA6 crypto-laundering service. These domains were used to register fraudulent KYC accounts at cryptocurrency exchanges; a corporate device touching them indicates either an insider acting as a money mule, attacker reuse of corporate infrastructure for laundering, or recruitment communications reaching staff. Rationale: All 19 domains are taken verbatim from the Europol statement in the article body — they are confirmed by a primary law-enforcement source naming them as AudiA6-controlled infrastructure for mule account registration. No second-source web search was performed; the IOC list IS the primary-source bulletin. The domains are unusual second-level / vanity TLDs (.pictures, .top, .click, .agency, .express, .black, .email) so corporate baseline noise is near-zero, justifying alerting tier.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the Europol seizure page or VirusTotal pivot from a security workstation
  • Compliance / fraud team performing mule-account research against the published domain list
  • Researcher visiting the post-takedown Europol seizure banner now hosted on the seized domains
  • Honeypot / sinkhole resolution sweeps from a security tooling host enumerating IOC lists
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountName !has_any ("soc","threatintel","fraud","compliance")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the resolving process and user — if InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser and the user belongs to security / fraud / compliance, check if they were actively reviewing the Europol bulletin (corroborate with browser history or ticket activity). Pull the device's user-context: insider risk score, finance/payments role, prior crypto-exchange traffic. Step 2 (contain): if the user is not a security researcher, isolate the device via Defender / Falcon Network Containment, suspend the AAD account, and block all 19 domains at the proxy/DNS layer pending review. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the device's last 30 days for outbound traffic to crypto-exchange APIs (binance, kraken, coinbase, kucoin), email to/from these same domains, and any KYC document uploads from the device; also sweep the org for any other host that resolved the same domain.
let AudiA6Domains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend HostLower = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where HostLower has_any (AudiA6Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let AudiA6Domains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | extend QueryLower = tolower(DnsQuery) | where QueryLower has_any (AudiA6Domains) | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Query = DnsQuery, ResponseCode = DnsResponseCodeName, Source = "ImDnsActivity"),
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | extend QueryLower = tolower(Name) | where QueryLower has_any (AudiA6Domains) | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname = Computer, SrcIpAddr = ClientIP, Query = Name, ResponseCode = ResultCode, Source = "DnsEvents")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound or outbound email involving AudiA6 mule-recruitment domains AIDelivery High
Detects email events where the sender or recipient domain matches one of the 19 AudiA6-controlled email domains identified by Europol. Article specifies these domains were used to register money-mule cryptocurrency exchange accounts using stolen identities and that Russian-speaking intermediaries were recruited via them — corporate email touching these domains indicates either mule-recruitment outreach or a staff member operating accounts on behalf of the laundering ring. Rationale: Article explicitly states AudiA6 'relied on both commercial email providers and email addresses linked to domains under their control to register money mule accounts' and recruited 'Russian-speaking intermediaries' via these channels — so inbound mail FROM these domains is recruitment outreach and outbound mail TO them is staff operating as mules. Sentinel KQL left empty because the provided Sentinel schema reference does not list a clean mailflow table (OfficeActivity covers admin operations, not full inbound metadata); operators on M365D-connected Sentinel tenants can re-use the Defender query verbatim against the imported EmailEvents table. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as none of those platforms ship M365 mailflow telemetry in the schemas referenced. Sigma skipped because Sigma's email logsource has no portable cross-vendor sender-domain selector matching this shape.
ATT&CKT1585.002 T1566
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Anti-fraud or threat-intel team mailing the AudiA6 domains for IOC validation / takedown coordination
  • A legitimate small SaaS that shared infrastructure on a generic vanity TLD (low risk given Europol seizure but possible for residual MX records on .email/.top domains)
  • Researcher subscribing a personal corporate mailbox to a blog newsletter that happens to send from one of the seized vanity domains pre-takedown
  • Quarantined / blocked spam that EmailEvents still records as a delivery attempt (DeliveryAction == Blocked) — analyst should treat these as a hit but lower severity
Suppression filter
| where not (RecipientEmailAddress has_any ("abuse@","soc@","threatintel@","fraud@") and EmailDirection == "Inbound")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full message body via Threat Explorer / Content Search, check EmailDirection (Inbound = likely recruitment, Outbound = potential mule activity by the user). Examine sender display name, language (article notes Russian-speaking intermediaries), and any crypto-wallet addresses or exchange-platform links in the body. Step 2 (contain): if Outbound from an internal user, suspend the AAD account and seize the mailbox for forensics; if Inbound and delivered, soft-delete from all recipient mailboxes via Threat Explorer and add the sender domain to the tenant block-list. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the recipient/sender user — pull their 90-day SigninLogs for unusual geo, AAD app consents to crypto-wallet/exchange OAuth apps, and any DLP hits on outbound files containing identity documents (passport scans, utility bills) which are the KYC artifacts AudiA6 needed for mule registration.
let AudiA6Domains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| extend SenderDom = tolower(SenderFromDomain), SenderMailDom = tolower(SenderMailFromDomain), RcptDom = tolower(tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress, "@")[1]))
| where SenderDom in (AudiA6Domains) or SenderMailDom in (AudiA6Domains) or RcptDom in (AudiA6Domains)
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, EmailDirection, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes, UrlCount, AttachmentCount
| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")

ShinyHunters Exploits Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day (CVE-2026-35273) to Breach Universities

The Hacker NewsCISA KEV
2026-06-12 17 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion crew exploited an unpatched flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft to break into enterprise systems, steal data, and demand payment to keep it private. The campaign hit universities hardest. Google's Mandiant attributes it to the group it tracks as UNC6240, and dates the activity between May 27 and June 9. Oracle did not publish its advisory until June 10, so the bug was a

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ShinyHunters staging-server IP connections — SimpleHTTP on TCP/8888 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PeopleSoft CVE-2026-35273 exploit — POST to /PSEMHUB/hub or /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ShinyHunters Exploits Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day (CVE-2026-35273) to Breach Univ

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Unexpected .jsp files written under PSEMHUB.war web application · [LLM] PeopleSoft XMLDecoder persistence — XML file changes under envmetadata/data/environment · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MeshCentral agent disguised as Microsoft Azure binary calling azurenetfiles.net · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ShinyHunters ransom marker file — README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT in PeopleSoft directories · [LLM] PeopleSoft lateral-movement script — *_fanout.sh execution and zstd compression chain · [LLM] Outbound SMB 445 from PeopleSoft host — NetNTLM hash capture · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
PeopleSoft CVE-2026-35273 exploit — POST to /PSEMHUB/hub or /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector AIExploitation Medium
Hunts external HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to the PSEMHUB and HttpListeningConnector endpoints, which Mandiant flagged as the CVE-2026-35273 entry point. The article specifically tells defenders to mine WebLogic access logs for these URIs because WAF body-inspection is bypassable. Rationale: Article body explicitly tells defenders to grep WebLogic access logs for external POST requests to /PSEMHUB/hub or /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector — Oracle's mitigation also points at these two paths. Internal CIDR exclusion knocks out admin testing. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • legitimate inbound PeopleSoft integrations from partner universities posting to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector
  • internal admin POSTing to /PSEMHUB/hub during environment-management maintenance
  • WAF or reverse-proxy health probes that emit POSTs
  • pentest / red-team activity against the same endpoints
  • Oracle Support-driven diagnostic POSTs from My Oracle Support tooling
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "OracleSupport" and cIP !in (dynamic(["partner_integration_ip_1","partner_integration_ip_2"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check `cIP` reputation, ASN, and prior history of POSTing to the host; pull the matching POST body from the WAF/reverse-proxy if body-logging is on. 2) Contain: if external, immediately block /PSEMHUB/* and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector at the perimeter per Oracle's CVE-2026-35273 guidance, then disable PSEMHUB on multi-server setups or remove the application on single-server. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceFileEvents for new .jsp files under PSEMHUB.war and XML changes under envmetadata/data/environment; check DeviceNetworkEvents for callbacks to the staging-IP block and azurenetfiles.net.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("HttpConnectionInspected","ConnectionInspected")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub","/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
let psemhub_paths = dynamic(["/PSEMHUB/hub","/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector"]);
let internal_cidrs = dynamic(["10.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.2","172.30.","172.31.","192.168."]);
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any (psemhub_paths)
| where not(cIP startswith_cs "10." or cIP startswith_cs "172.16." or cIP startswith_cs "172.17." or cIP startswith_cs "192.168.")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters staging-server IP connections — SimpleHTTP on TCP/8888 AIDelivery Medium
Catches inbound or outbound traffic to/from the five sequential Mandiant-tracked staging IPs running Python SimpleHTTP on TCP/8888. These IPs hosted the .bash_history, fake-Azure MeshCentral agents, and the fanout script — any session is high-fidelity. Rationale: All seven IPs were enumerated in the article (five sequential staging IPs + two adjacent — Mandiant said they ran SimpleHTTPServer on 8888). Single-event-shape IP IOC — single source confirmation OK because the article quotes Mandiant attributing them directly. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • security researcher curl/wget testing the published IPs
  • internal threat-intel tooling validating IOCs
  • TI feed enrichment process making test connections
  • honeypot or sandbox detonations reaching the same IPs
  • VPN egress IP overlap if any of these are shared infrastructure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","otx-cli.exe","opencti-worker.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "TI-RESEARCH"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which host initiated the connection, what process (`InitiatingProcessFileName`), and whether the host runs PeopleSoft/WebLogic. 2) Contain: block all seven IPs at the perimeter, isolate the initiating host, capture memory and disk image before reboot. 3) Hunt: search for MeshCentral binaries masquerading as Microsoft Azure, callbacks to azurenetfiles.net, the README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT marker, and outbound 445 SMB from PeopleSoft hosts.
let staging_ips = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);

| order by Timestamp desc

CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationIP in (staging_ips) or SourceIP in (staging_ips)
| where DestinationPort == 8888 or SourcePort == 8888 or isempty(tostring(DestinationPort))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction, RequestURL, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName

Unexpected .jsp files written under PSEMHUB.war web application AIInstallation High
Mandiant's hunting guidance calls out unexpected .jsp files dropped into the PSEMHUB.war directory and odd folders (logs, persistantstorage, scratchpad) under PSEMHUB paths. A new JSP under PSEMHUB is post-exploit webshell territory. Rationale: Article explicitly lists "Unexpected .jsp files under the PSEMHUB.war web application directory, or odd folders named logs, persistantstorage, or scratchpad under the PSEMHUB paths" as a Mandiant hunting indicator — exact strings. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Oracle PeopleTools patch deployment adding legitimate .jsp files (verify against My Oracle Support patch metadata)
  • internal developer hotfix push touching PSEMHUB pages
  • PeopleSoft application server caching/temp file expansion into scratchpad
  • backup or AV scanning agent emitting file-create events through hardlinks
  • configuration management tool (Ansible/Puppet) rolling out a change
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","opatch.exe","opatch.bat","psadmin.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("opatch apply","patch_install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the .jsp content and SHA256, check signing/PeopleTools patch manifest, identify `InitiatingProcessFileName` writing the file. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the WebLogic host, snapshot the JVM heap. 3) Hunt: search for outbound connections from the WebLogic process to the seven staging IPs and azurenetfiles.net; pivot on the writing process and look for XMLDecoder XML changes under envmetadata.

PeopleSoft XMLDecoder persistence — XML file changes under envmetadata/data/environment AIInstallation High
Hunts XML file changes under the WebLogic doc-root path envmetadata/data/environment — Mandiant calls out this path as an XMLDecoder persistence sink that fires on the next server restart. Rationale: Article body verbatim: "Recently changed .xml files under the web doc root's envmetadata/data/environment, which can be abused for XMLDecoder persistence that fires on the next restart" — exact path string. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • legitimate PeopleSoft environment-management push from PSEMHUB clients refreshing inventory XML
  • Oracle patch deployment rewriting environment metadata
  • scheduled environment sync job (Update Gateway uploads)
  • DR / backup restore re-populating envmetadata
  • PeopleTools upgrade migration tasks
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("PS","PSADMIN","oracle") or ActingProcessName !in~ ("opatch","opatch.bat","opatch.exe","psadmin")
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the modified XML against version-control or yesterday's backup, looking for `<java>` / `<object class="java.beans.XMLDecoder">` / `Runtime.exec` gadgets. 2) Contain: restore the XML from a known-good backup, restart WebLogic after, snapshot the JVM before restart for forensic capture. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process — if it's the WebLogic JVM with no admin shell parent, that's the exploit chain; check outbound to staging IPs immediately.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "envmetadata" and FolderPath has "environment"
| where FileName endswith ".xml"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has "envmetadata" and TargetFilePath has "environment"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "xml"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MeshCentral agent disguised as Microsoft Azure binary calling azurenetfiles.net AICommand & Control High
ShinyHunters dropped custom MeshCentral remote-management agents disguised as Microsoft Azure binaries that called home to azurenetfiles.net — a typosquat of Azure NetApp Files. Hunts DNS or HTTP to the C2 domain and the Azure-impersonating binaries. Rationale: Article names the domain verbatim — "azurenetfiles.net, a domain picked to look like Azure NetApp Files" — and ties it to custom MeshCentral agents disguised as Microsoft Azure binaries. Single domain IOC, single-event-shape. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Network_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • security researcher / threat-intel passive DNS resolution
  • sandbox detonation reaching the domain
  • DNS sinkhole resolving the domain to a controlled IP (still legitimate hit)
  • TI feed enrichment job
  • internal validation of published IOCs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp-worker","otx-cli","opencti-worker.exe","vmtoolsd.exe") and DvcHostname !startswith "TI-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the initiating process binary, hash it, compare metadata `InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName` (should NOT actually be Microsoft if it's the fake-Azure MeshCentral). 2) Contain: sinkhole azurenetfiles.net at the resolver, block the IP, isolate the host, capture memory. 3) Hunt: search the host for MeshCentral binaries with Microsoft Azure metadata, check for the fanout.sh script, look at outbound SSH/SMB from the same host.
let c2_domain = "azurenetfiles.net";
let net = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has c2_domain
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, SHA256=InitiatingProcessSHA256;
let dns = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
    | where RemoteUrl has c2_domain
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl;
union net, dns
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2 = "azurenetfiles.net";
let dns_hits = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has c2
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DstIpAddr;
let web_hits = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Url has c2 or HttpHostName has c2
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent;
union dns_hits, web_hits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters ransom marker file — README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT in PeopleSoft directories AIActions on Objectives High
The fanout.sh script drops a marker file literally named README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT into PeopleSoft directories after spreading. Exact string match — zero ambiguity. Rationale: Article quotes the exact filename: "drops a marker file named README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT into PeopleSoft directories". Zero false-positive risk — no legitimate system writes this filename. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657/
ATT&CKT1657 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR team copying the IOC sample to a lab host for analysis
  • security awareness exercise / tabletop simulating the breach
  • honeypot file-bait creation by detection-tuning engineers
  • antivirus signature deployment containing the filename as a string
  • git repo containing the IOC list cloned to a workstation
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !startswith "IR-LAB" and DvcHostname !startswith "SANDBOX"
Response runbook
1) Triage: immediately treat as confirmed compromise — read the file content, hash it, snapshot the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host network, freeze the PeopleSoft application, snapshot the WebLogic JVM and any database connections in progress. 3) Hunt: trace the writing process backwards through fanout.sh execution, identify the source SSH session, find every host the script reached via /etc/hosts, look for zstd compression activity and outbound SSH to ShinyHunters leak-mirror infrastructure.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PeopleSoft lateral-movement script — *_fanout.sh execution and zstd compression chain AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of the [victim]_fanout.sh lateral-movement script and the zstd-then-SSH exfil chain Mandiant pulled from the attackers' shared .bash_history. Targets Linux/PeopleSoft hosts where this chain runs. Rationale: Article: "The script, named [victim]_fanout.sh, spreads over SSH by spraying a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords against internal hosts pulled from /etc/hosts" and "data compressed with zstd and an outbound SSH connection to the server hosting the public mirror of the ShinyHunters leak site". Filename pattern + tool names are article-grounded. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1560/001/
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1110.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • sysadmin running a homemade fan-out deploy script that happens to be named *_fanout.sh
  • Ansible/Puppet sync push using ssh fan-out helpers
  • backup compression with zstd against application directories (verify path scope)
  • internal /etc/hosts-based health-check ping scripts
  • DevOps tooling that orchestrates parallel SSH
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef","saltstack","deploy") and ActingProcessName !in~ ("ansible-playbook","puppet-agent")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the running script body (`cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `lsof -p <pid>`), enumerate the SSH child processes and destination hosts; check `/etc/hosts` for the candidate list. 2) Contain: kill the parent shell, rotate every credential in the hardcoded list, block SSH egress from the compromised host. 3) Hunt: pull `bash_history` from every host the script touched, look for the README marker, check egress to staging IPs and azurenetfiles.net, search for zstd archives staged in /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)_fanout\.sh")
   or (FileName =~ "zstd" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSEMHUB","peoplesoft","/u01","/opt/oracle"))
   or (FileName =~ "sshpass" and ProcessCommandLine has "/etc/hosts")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh") and TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)_fanout\.sh")
     or (TargetProcessName =~ "zstd" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSEMHUB","peoplesoft","/u01","/opt/oracle"))
     or (TargetProcessName =~ "sshpass" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "/etc/hosts")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: e5f6a7b8-c9d0-1e2f-3a4b-5c6d7e8f9012
description: Execution of *_fanout.sh lateral-movement script or zstd compression over PeopleSoft directories — observed in ShinyHunters .bash_history captured by Mandiant
references:

| (CommandLine=/_fanout\.sh/i)
  OR (ImageFileName=/\/zstd$/i AND CommandLine=/(PSEMHUB|peoplesoft|\/u01\/|\/opt\/oracle\/)/i)
  OR (ImageFileName=/\/sshpass$/i AND CommandLine=/\/etc\/hosts/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Outbound SMB 445 from PeopleSoft host — NetNTLM hash capture AIActions on Objectives High
Mandiant's hunting list flags outbound SMB (TCP/445) from PeopleSoft hosts to external destinations as part of the CVE-2026-35273 exploit chain — used to coerce machine-account NetNTLM hashes out of the server. Any non-RFC1918 destination on 445 from a PeopleSoft host is high signal. Rationale: Article: "Outbound SMB traffic on port 445 from PeopleSoft hosts to external destinations, which the exploit chain may use to capture machine-account NetNTLM hashes" — direct port and direction guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1187/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001/
ATT&CKT1187 T1557.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • legitimate cloud SMB mounts (Azure Files / FSx) reachable via public endpoints
  • SMB-over-internet to a partner file-share appliance
  • misconfigured backup uploads using SMB to a cloud target
  • VPN-split-tunnel scenario where the public path is taken
  • user opening an obfuscated UNC link in a phishing email
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup-agent.exe","azcopy.exe","AzureFilesAgent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if it's the WebLogic Java process or psadmin, treat as exploit-chain confirmed. 2) Contain: block egress 445 to the destination IP at the perimeter, isolate the host, force machine-account password rotation. 3) Hunt: pull packet capture if available for hash extraction, correlate to inbound POSTs against /PSEMHUB/hub at the same time, sweep all PeopleSoft hosts for the same egress pattern.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 445 and Protocol == "Tcp"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 445
| where NetworkProtocol =~ "TCP" or isempty(NetworkProtocol)
| where not(DstIpAddr startswith "10." or DstIpAddr startswith "172.16." or DstIpAddr startswith "172.17." or DstIpAddr startswith "172.18." or DstIpAddr startswith "172.19." or DstIpAddr startswith "172.2" or DstIpAddr startswith "172.30." or DstIpAddr startswith "172.31." or DstIpAddr startswith "192.168." or DstIpAddr startswith "127.")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Talos prevalent malware hash dropped to disk (DeviceFileEvents pivot)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos weekly prevalent malware hash execution (Coinminer/Injector/Dropper.Miner) · [LLM] Talos prevalent malware filename pattern — VID001.exe and d4aa3e70..._N_Exe.exe · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Talos weekly prevalent malware hash execution (Coinminer/Injector/Dropper.Miner) AIInstallation High
Detects process execution where the binary's SHA256 or MD5 matches one of the four hashes Talos flagged in this week's prevalent-malware roundup — Win.Worm.Coinminer::1201 (VID001.exe), W32.Injector:Gen.21ie.1201, and Win.Dropper.Miner::95.sbx.tg. Hash-only match keeps fidelity high. Rationale: Pure IOC match against the four SHA256/MD5 pairs Talos published in the 2026-06-11 prevalent-malware list — Win.Worm.Coinminer::1201 (9f1f11a7...), W32.Injector:Gen.21ie.1201 (96fa6a77...), Win.Dropper.Miner::95.sbx.tg (a31f222f...), and the fourth truncated SHA256. Hash-only match is the highest-fidelity signal available from this newsletter. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1496 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IR / malware-analysis sandbox detonating samples for research
  • Threat-hunting team intentionally executing IOC samples in a contained lab to test detections
  • AV/EDR product unpacking a sample as part of a deep-scan task (process is the AV engine, not the malware)
  • Hash collision (mathematically negligible at SHA256, but possible at MD5 for the four MD5s — corroborate against SHA256 before escalating)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("SANDBOX-001", "MALWARE-LAB-01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe", "CSFalconService.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm SHA256 (not MD5 alone) match. Pull Talos File Reputation lookup for the matched hash; check DeviceName isolation status and whether the host is a known sandbox/analyst workstation. Capture full ProcessCommandLine, parent chain, and AccountName. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device via Defender 'Isolate machine' or equivalent EDR action; block the SHA256 at the org IOC indicator list (Defender ASR/Indicators) to prevent re-execution on other hosts. Suspend the account if the binary executed under user context. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 to find the dropper; sweep DeviceNetworkEvents for mining-pool ports (3333, 4444, 5555, 7777, 14444) from the same DeviceId in the past 14 days; sweep DeviceFileEvents for the matched SHA256 to find all drop locations and earliest-seen timestamp across the estate.

Talos prevalent malware hash dropped to disk (DeviceFileEvents pivot) AIDelivery Medium
Catches the file-drop / staging phase before execution — flags any file write whose SHA256 or MD5 matches the Talos 2026-06-11 prevalent-malware list. Pivoting on DeviceFileEvents surfaces the dropper that wrote the binary, even if the payload never executes. Rationale: Targets the file-write phase rather than execution — same Talos 2026-06-11 hash IOCs but pivoting on DeviceFileEvents/Sysmon-11/FileWritten. Catches droppers that stage the payload but never run it (or run it after a long delay), which the execution-time UC would miss. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91
ATT&CKT1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender / EDR quarantine action writing the file to a quarantine folder (e.g. C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Quarantine) — hash matches but file is contained
  • SOC / IR team copying a sample into an analysis share for hunting purposes
  • Backup product (Veeam, CrashPlan) restoring a previously-quarantined sample from snapshot
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline (MISP, OpenCTI) writing IOC samples into a managed corpus directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe", "CSFalconService.exe", "sense.exe") and FolderPath !contains @"\Quarantine\" and FolderPath !contains @"\Malware-Lab\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the drop site (FolderPath) and the dropper (InitiatingProcessFileName + InitiatingProcessCommandLine). Check FileOriginUrl / FileOriginIP to determine whether the file came from web download, USB, or lateral copy. Step 2 — Contain: delete the dropped file (or confirm quarantine), block the SHA256 at the Defender Indicators list, and block FileOriginUrl/FileOriginIP at the proxy/firewall if external. Isolate the host if the dropper is unsigned or unknown. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the estate to find all hosts that ran the same dropper; sweep DeviceProcessEvents for the dropped SHA256 to confirm whether the payload also executed (chain to UC1); review FileOriginUrl history for the dropper to identify the source campaign.
