npm publish / login / auth-token write from a developer endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces npm auth and publish CLI activity plus .npmrc credential-file writes on workstations - the precursor to a package-hijack supply-chain attack. Splits the original (broken) single-column lookup into a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents so neither query references a non-canonical column. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain risk, but credential write + publish from a developer endpoint is how a package gets hijacked at source. Hunts for npm publish/login/token CLI flows and .npmrc credential-file writes (which carry _authToken=). Uses canonical Defender columns only - replaces the previous query that referenced a non-existent NpmrcWrites column with a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/npmrc
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package authors running npm publish to a private registry as part of normal workflow
  • Onboarding flows that create ~/.npmrc with corporate registry tokens
  • CI agents publishing release artifacts on tag push
  • Developers running npm whoami / npm login after rotating their npm token
  • IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains) writing project-local .npmrc files
Suppression filter
| where not (Initiator has_any ("actions-runner","gitlab-runner","TeamCity","Jenkins","agent.exe") and EventKind == "npm_auth_cli")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user is an authorized package publisher; for .npmrc writes, read the file and look for _authToken=, registry overrides, or always-auth=true on non-corporate hosts. 2) Contain: if unauthorized publish, immediately revoke the npm token (npm token revoke) and the user's npmjs.com session; if a malicious package version was published, contact npm security to deprecate/unpublish and notify downstream consumers. 3) Hunt: pivot on the username across npm registry audit logs for prior publishes; check whether the same .npmrc token appears on other endpoints; look for outbound POSTs to registry.npmjs.org/_token or /-/v1/login from the same host in the last 24h.
let NpmAuth = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=ProcessCommandLine, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let NpmrcChange = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=strcat(FolderPath,"\\",FileName), Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
NpmAuth
| union NpmrcChange
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=CommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=TargetFilePath)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*"npm publish"* OR *"npm login"* OR *"npm adduser"* OR *"npm token create"* OR *"npm token revoke"*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.NPMRC))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(npm\\s+(publish|login|adduser|whoami)|npm\\s+token\\s+(create|revoke))", field=CommandLine)) OR (#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\.npmrc$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
npm install with --ignore-scripts=false or NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS override AIWeaponization High
Catches explicit attempts to re-enable lifecycle scripts that npm 12 disables by default - via --ignore-scripts=false CLI flag, NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false env var, or the new approve-scripts opt-in path. After the v12 upgrade rolls out, an adversary with code-exec on a developer box needs to flip this back on to land lifecycle-based persistence. Rationale: Article explicitly names --ignore-scripts as the flag npm 12's new default replaces, and references npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as the opt-in. NPM_CONFIG_* envvar form is documented npm config behavior. After the v12 ramp, any of these strings on a developer endpoint is an adversary opting out of the new default. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/config
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as instructed by the GitHub blog during upgrade prep
  • Build scripts that legitimately set NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false for native-module builds
  • Dockerfile RUN lines that force --foreground-scripts for log visibility
  • Internal tooling that wraps npm and passes the flag through transparently
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "allow-scripts-pending" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName endswith "\\explorer.exe" and AccountName has_any ("dev","engineer","build"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user, package set, and whether this was the documented upgrade-prep approve-scripts flow vs a fresh install with the flag flipped. Pull surrounding child processes within +/- 60s. 2) Contain: if not approved, isolate the host and capture node_modules for the project; revoke any tokens present in .npmrc. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same flag pattern in the last 30 days, look for the same flag combined with --registry pointing off-mainstream, and check whether the same user/host hit UC1 (lifecycle-script suspicious child) in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Baileys messages.upsert with requestId field — exploitation marker (CVE-2026-48063) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-48063 in Baileys (WhatsApp Web library) by hunting for the application-log signature documented in the advisory's workaround section: a messages.upsert event carrying a requestId field. The advisory tells defenders to drop exactly these events as the only practical mitigation, so their presence on a vulnerable build is a direct exploitation marker. Rationale: Advisory 'Workarounds' section explicitly names dropping messages.upsert events that contain a requestId field as the only real workaround — making that exact field combination the highest-fidelity exploitation signature the article gives us. Cross-referenced patch commit 3beb08ee and the GHSA advisory page. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1566.003 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Already-patched Baileys (>=7.0.0-rc12 / >=6.7.22) still emitting a benign requestId on legitimate placeholderResendMessage flows during normal history recovery
  • Custom Baileys forks that legitimately use requestId for in-house tracing/observability tagging
  • QA / staging debug logs where placeholderResendMessage is intentionally fuzzed to test resilience
  • Alternative WA libraries (whatsapp-web.js, venom-bot) emitting the substring 'messages.upsert' in their own log shape without the Baileys vuln
Suppression filter
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("version=7.0.0-rc12", "version=7.0.0-rc13", "version=6.7.22", "version=6.7.23"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the Baileys version on the alerting host (npm ls baileys / cat node_modules/baileys/package.json). If <7.0.0-rc12 or <6.7.22, treat the requestId-bearing upsert as an exploitation attempt; capture the SyslogMessage and the offending requestId for IR. Step 2 — Contain: terminate the Node.js process owning the WA socket and revoke the linked-device session inside the WhatsApp mobile app — this invalidates the attacker's spoofing channel and forces re-pair. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate every host running the vulnerable npm package; pivot on the requestId pattern across 30 days of forwarded app logs to find earlier silent spoofing that the upsert handler accepted.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessId, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("node", "nodejs", "pm2") or SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert" and SyslogMessage has "requestId"

Baileys app state sync corruption — repeated reconciliation failures from a single peer AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the second documented impact of CVE-2026-48063: 'corrupt the app state sync system by sending fake key shares'. Hunts for clusters of app-state-sync validation errors, key-share rejections, or sync rollbacks emitted by Baileys-based Node.js services within a short window — the cascading-correction pattern the advisory describes. Rationale: Advisory Impact paragraph explicitly cites 'corrupt the app state sync system by sending fake key shares' and 'no workarounds for the app state sync jamming' — making clusters of app-state-sync failures the natural detectable signature of the second exploit path. Anchor strings (appStateSync, AppStateSyncKey, fetchAppStateSyncKey) come from the public Baileys source tree referenced by patch commit 3beb08ee. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network instability causing transient WA socket disconnects and benign appStateSync retries
  • Legitimate bulk-message flows that trigger normal sync reconciliation
  • Account using multiple linked devices simultaneously, producing concurrent appStateSync deltas
  • Baileys upgrade in progress where a new key-share format temporarily mismatches cached state
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the host runs a vulnerable Baileys version (<7.0.0-rc12 / <6.7.22). If yes and >=3 appStateSync failures occurred in <10 min from the same session, treat as exploitation. Step 2 — Contain: stop the affected Node.js service, wipe the local Baileys auth/keys directory, and re-pair via QR / 8-digit code from the mobile device. Do NOT restore from snapshot — local state may already be corrupted. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the WA session ID / Baileys auth folder across all other hosts using shared credentials; check for messages.upsert + requestId hits (UC1) on the same time window.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| summarize ProcessStarts = count(), FirstStart = min(Timestamp), LastStart = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ProcessStarts >= 3
| order by LastStart desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("appStateSync", "AppStateSyncKey", "app-state-sync", "syncAppState", "fetchAppStateSyncKey")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("fail", "error", "invalid", "rollback", "reject", "mismatch", "timeout")
| summarize FailCount = count(), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FailCount >= 3
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") AND (appStateSync OR AppStateSyncKey OR fetchAppStateSyncKey OR syncAppState) AND (fail OR error OR invalid OR rollback OR reject OR mismatch)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName="*node.exe" OR ImageFileName="*/node")

| where fail_count >= 3

Vulnerable Baileys npm package presence (<7.0.0-rc12 / <6.7.22) — fleet inventory hunt AIWeaponization High
Identifies hosts with a vulnerable Baileys install on disk so the SOC can drive patch adoption for CVE-2026-48063. Pivots on node_modules/baileys and node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys package.json writes captured by EDR file telemetry. Escalates internet-facing services that remain unpatched >7 days post-advisory. Rationale: Article specifies the exact vulnerable npm package names (baileys, @whiskeysockets/baileys) and the version cut-offs (<7.0.0-rc12, <6.7.22). The file-event signature on node_modules/<pkg>/package.json is the most reliable cross-EDR fingerprint of installation regardless of host OS. Cross-checked the GHSA advisory and the npm registry pages. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://www.npmjs.com/package/baileys • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@whiskeysockets/baileys
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Already-patched installs (>=7.0.0-rc12 / >=6.7.22) — file presence alone doesn't reveal version; analyst must read package.json contents
  • Developer workstations with the package installed for local testing (lower severity than production hosts)
  • Containers built FROM a vulnerable layer but never run in production
  • Old node_modules trees inside a backup snapshot mounted on a sandbox host
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: for every alerting host, read node_modules/baileys/package.json (or @whiskeysockets variant) and extract the version field. Hosts on >=7.0.0-rc12 or >=6.7.22 are patched — close. Otherwise continue. Step 2 — Contain: prioritise internet-facing or production WA-bot services; schedule package upgrade via npm install baileys@^7.0.0-rc12 (or 6.7.22 for the v6 line) and redeploy. Step 3 — Hunt: cross-reference against UC1 (messages.upsert + requestId) and UC2 (appStateSync failures) on the same hosts to confirm whether exploitation already occurred before the patch lands.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" and FolderPath has "baileys"
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Writers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5) by DeviceName, FolderPath
| where LastSeen > ago(7d)
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules" and TargetFilePath has "baileys"
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath
| where LastSeen > ago(7d)
| order by LastSeen desc

Baileys Node.js exceptions during protocolMessage parsing — exploit-path indicator AIExploitation Medium
Detects malformed protocolMessage parsing failures inside Baileys-based services: TypeErrors, RangeErrors, buffer overruns, or unhandled promise rejections referencing protocolMessage or its decoder paths. The advisory pins the root cause to maliciously crafted protocolMessage payloads, so deserialisation exceptions on inbound payloads are an early-stage exploitation signal. Rationale: Article maps exploitation to a 'maliciously crafted protocolMessage payload' — clustered Node.js deserialisation exceptions referencing protocolMessage in Baileys-tagged log lines are the natural exploit-path telemetry. Exception strings (TypeError / RangeError / UnhandledPromiseRejection / ERR_BUFFER_OUT_OF_BOUNDS) are V8-canonical and emitted by every Node.js runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Baileys upgrade in flight — old serialised state on disk + new code triggers parsing exceptions on first launch
  • Truly malformed inbound messages from buggy peer clients (not exploit) that still throw RangeError on the wire
  • Unrelated Node.js exceptions on the same process that mention 'TypeError' but aren't in the Baileys protocolMessage path
  • Local development environments with verbose debug logging producing benign caught-and-logged exceptions
Suppression filter
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("DeprecationWarning", "ExperimentalWarning", "npm WARN"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the stack trace from the offending SyslogMessage; confirm the failing frame is inside Baileys (node_modules/baileys/lib/Socket/messages-recv or similar). If yes, treat as exploitation attempt. Step 2 — Contain: stop the affected Node.js service to halt continued exploitation of the same payload pattern; capture the inbound raw message buffer if logged for IR sample. Step 3 — Hunt: correlate the exception timestamp with UC1 (messages.upsert + requestId) within 60s; sweep across all Baileys hosts for the same stack frame to find scaled exploitation attempts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| summarize ProcessStarts = count(), FirstStart = min(Timestamp), LastStart = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ProcessStarts >= 3
| order by LastStart desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys", "protocolMessage")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("TypeError", "RangeError", "SyntaxError", "UnhandledPromiseRejection", "Cannot read prop", "out of range", "ERR_BUFFER_OUT_OF_BOUNDS")
| summarize ExcCount = count(), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where ExcCount >= 2
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys" OR protocolMessage) AND (TypeError OR RangeError OR UnhandledPromiseRejection OR "Cannot read prop" OR "out of range")
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName="*node.exe" OR ImageFileName="*/node")
| regex("baileys|whiskeysockets", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RawProcessId, CommandLine], function=count(as=launches))
| launches > 3
APPLICATION
index=app OR index=nodejs OR index=application (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys" OR "protocolMessage") ("TypeError" OR "RangeError" OR "SyntaxError" OR "UnhandledPromiseRejection" OR "Cannot read prop" OR "out of range" OR "ERR_BUFFER_OUT_OF_BOUNDS")
| bin _time span=5m as bucket

Fake messages.upsert from unknown peer JID — Baileys session-list anomaly AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the spoofed-message impact of CVE-2026-48063: messages.upsert events whose source peer JID isn't part of the established Baileys session peer list, or where decryption/MAC verification failed but the upsert still fired. These are the article's 'fake message key and payload' artefacts that the patch in commit 3beb08ee now rejects. Rationale: Advisory states the exploit lets an attacker 'trigger a fake messages.upsert event with a fake message key and payload' — the natural signature is upsert log lines accompanied by peer-list or cryptographic-verification failures emitted by Baileys (the patch in commit 3beb08ee adds exactly these rejection paths). Anchor strings (verifyMessage, decryption failed, MAC verification, remoteJid mismatch, unknown jid) come from Baileys' source tree and Signal-protocol-derived error vocabulary. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1566.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Group chat where a participant left and rejoined causing a transient JID-not-in-session warning
  • Mobile device re-pair while the Baileys session was active producing benign decryption-failed lines
  • Bot temporarily disconnected during sender-key rotation, replaying with stale state
  • Custom Baileys patches that intentionally log verifyMessage warnings without dropping the event
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: extract the offending JID from the SyslogMessage; check whether it appears anywhere else in the host's WA session history. If never seen, treat as spoof. Step 2 — Contain: terminate the Baileys Node.js process, revoke the linked-device in the WhatsApp mobile app, and wipe local auth/keys before re-pair. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the spoofed JID across all hosts using the same WA number; cross-reference against UC1 hits and UC4 exception bursts in the same time window — a clean triple-positive is a confirmed exploitation chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("web.whatsapp.com", "g.whatsapp.net", "mmg.whatsapp.net") or RemotePort in (443, 5222)
| summarize WaConnections = count(), Peers = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where WaConnections > 0
| order by bin_Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("unknown jid", "jid not in session", "unknown peer", "verifyMessage", "decryption failed", "MAC verification", "remoteJid mismatch", "unrecognised participant")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") AND "messages.upsert" AND ("unknown jid" OR "jid not in session" OR "unknown peer" OR verifyMessage OR "decryption failed" OR "MAC verification" OR "remoteJid mismatch")
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=5222) ContextImageFileName="*node*"
| regex("baileys|whiskeysockets", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count(as=connections))
APPLICATION
index=app OR index=nodejs OR index=application (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") "messages.upsert" ("unknown jid" OR "jid not in session" OR "unknown peer" OR "verifyMessage" OR "decryption failed" OR "MAC verification" OR "remoteJid mismatch" OR "unrecognised participant")
| stats count as anomalies values(source) as sources first(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen by host process
| where anomalies >= 1

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    product: windows
detection:

            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

China-Linked JDY Botnet Expands to 1,500+ Devices for Cyber Reconnaissance

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have warned of a "resurgence and expansion" of JDY, a covert network associated with China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors. "The JDY botnet comprises over 1,500 SOHO [small office and home office] and IoT devices and operates as a centrally controlled, high-performance scanner used to discover, fingerprint, and continuously map exposed services at scale," Lumen's

CVEsCVE-2026-35616
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1528

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] High-fanout TCP SYN scanning sourced from internal SOHO/IoT subnet · [LLM] Mass internal-recon command bursts across multiple hosts · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] JDY MIPS architecture payload download via shell script dropper · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Coordinated periodic beaconing fanout across many internal devices · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
High-fanout TCP SYN scanning sourced from internal SOHO/IoT subnet AIReconnaissance High
Hunts the article's most distinctive JDY behaviour: a single internal host opening raw-socket SYN scans against a large fan-out of distinct external IP/port pairs. Per the Lumen report, JDY uses 'custom-crafted TCP packets' for high-speed SYN scanning when the malware has raw-socket access — the network pattern is fan-out without follow-on payload. Rationale: Article: 'If it can open a raw socket, an indication of root privileges, it initiates high-speed SYN scanning using custom-crafted TCP packets.' Detection captures the network signature (high fanout, low/no establishment) regardless of agent presence on the SOHO/IoT device itself — most consumer routers/cameras don't run Defender, so we hunt at the perimeter and on any segment that mirrors traffic. Sigma omitted because the detection is a count/threshold aggregation, not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1046/
ATT&CKT1046 T1595.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus / Qualys / Tenable scan engine) sweeping internet-facing assets
  • Network monitoring tool (Zabbix / SolarWinds / PRTG) doing reachability probes
  • Misconfigured VOIP appliance hammering SIP registrars across many providers
  • Crashlooping application opening + retrying many outbound sockets during failure
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["10.0.10.50","10.0.10.51"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the source IP's DHCP lease + DeviceInfo to identify the asset class; check if it's in the authorised scanner allowlist (Nessus, Qualys, Tenable); sample 50 of the destination IPs and check whether they sit on a vulnerability-disclosure surface (recently-CVE'd products) — JDY targets newly-disclosed vulns. Step 2 — Contain: if not an authorised scanner, isolate at the switch; preserve a tcpdump of next 5 minutes of traffic if possible — packet timing + raw-socket fingerprint distinguishes JDY's custom TCP from off-the-shelf nmap. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source IP for outbound 9001/9030/9050/9150 (Tor) in the last 24h; check DeviceProcessEvents on any agent-covered hosts on the same /24 for shell-script dropper artifacts (mips/mips64/mipsel/mipsel64 binaries written to /tmp and immediately deleted); query egress for the JDY shell-dropper download patterns.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where Protocol =~ "Tcp"
| summarize DistinctDestIPs = dcount(RemoteIP), DistinctDestPorts = dcount(RemotePort), AttemptCount = count(), TopPorts = make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctDestIPs > 200 and DistinctDestPorts > 10
| order by DistinctDestIPs desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where NetworkProtocol =~ "TCP"
| where NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound"
| where EventResult =~ "Failure" or DvcAction in~ ("Deny","Drop","Reject")
| summarize DistinctDestIPs = dcount(DstIpAddr), DistinctDestPorts = dcount(DstPortNumber), AttemptCount = count(), TopPorts = make_set(DstPortNumber, 20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctDestIPs > 200 and DistinctDestPorts > 10
| order by DistinctDestIPs desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Protocol:tcp -@Image:(*\nmap.exe OR *\masscan.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| Protocol=6
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, bucket(span=10m)], function={ DistinctIPs := count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true) | DistinctPorts := count(field=RemotePort, distinct=true) | Attempts := count() })
| DistinctIPs > 200
| DistinctPorts > 10
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
# VPC Flow Logs use different schema than CloudTrail (srcaddr, dstaddr, srcport, dstport, protocol, action).
# Hunt for high-fanout SYN-like patterns: many REJECT records from a single source to many distinct destinations.
# Field paths here follow the standard VPC Flow log JSON shape; if your VPC flow logs land in a custom format, adjust the parse stage.
fields @timestamp, @message
| parse @message "* * * * * * * * * * * * * *" as version, account, eni, srcaddr, dstaddr, srcport, dstport, protocol, packets, bytes, start, end, action, logstatus
| filter action = "REJECT" and protocol = "6"
| stats count(*) as attempts, count_distinct(dstaddr) as distinct_dst, count_distinct(dstport) as distinct_ports by srcaddr, bin(10m)
| filter distinct_dst > 200 and distinct_ports > 10
| sort distinct_dst desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as DistinctDestIPs dc(All_Traffic.dest_port) as DistinctDestPorts count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.action="blocked" OR All_Traffic.tcp_flag="SYN" by All_Traffic.src_ip _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")` | where DistinctDestIPs > 200 AND DistinctDestPorts > 10 | sort - DistinctDestIPs
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as DistinctDestIPs dc(All_Traffic.dest_port) as DistinctDestPorts count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.action="blocked" OR All_Traffic.tcp_flag="SYN" by All_Traffic.src_ip _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")` | where DistinctDestIPs > 200 AND DistinctDestPorts > 10 | sort - DistinctDestIPs
JDY MIPS architecture payload download via shell script dropper AIDelivery High
Hunts the article's described JDY infection chain: a shell-script dropper that runs an arch check then downloads a per-architecture payload (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64). Targets Linux-class telemetry (auditd, syslog) on edge/IoT/server estate. Self-deletion after launch is part of the same artefact chain. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'download the primary payload based on the detected processor architecture (e.g., mips, mips64, mipsel, or mipsel64). Once the malware is launched, it's deleted from disk.' The arch-string + downloader combo is uniquely JDY-shaped — these CPU strings rarely appear together with wget/curl outside of IoT-malware contexts. Cross-checked against KV-botnet / Volt Typhoon reporting where same MIPS targeting is documented. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1017/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-038a
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OpenWrt / DD-WRT firmware build pipeline downloading cross-arch toolchains
  • Embedded developer pulling busybox cross-compile artifacts to a Linux dev box
  • Yocto / Buildroot CI runner fetching MIPS sysroot tarballs
  • Educational malware-analysis lab on a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in (dynamic(["openwrt-build-01","yocto-ci-01","malware-sandbox-01"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the host class — IoT/edge appliance, container, dev workstation, or sandbox? Pull recent ImFileEvent records for files written to /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm in the 5 minutes around the alert; if a file was written and then deleted (no follow-up FileAccessed) that matches JDY's self-deletion pattern. Step 2 — Contain: if production host, isolate at the network layer; preserve /proc/$pid/maps and /proc/$pid/exe for any process whose backing file is unlinked — those are the still-running JDY scanner instances. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the source IP of the wget/curl/tftp call against threat-intel for JDY C2; sweep the rest of the estate for the same download URL using ImFileEvent / DeviceFileEvents over the last 30d; check whether CVE-2026-35616 affects the device class in question and whether it's patched.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","ash","dash","busybox")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mipsel64","mipsel","mips64"," mips ")
   and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wget","curl","tftp","ftpget","busybox wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","ash","dash","busybox")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("mipsel64","mipsel","mips64"," mips ")
   and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("wget","curl","tftp","ftpget")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JDY Botnet MIPS Architecture Payload Dropper
id: 6a3e8c1d-7f42-4b3c-9d2e-8f1a5c2b3d4e
description: Detects the JDY botnet shell-script dropper that performs CPU architecture detection (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) before downloading the architecture-matched payload via wget/curl/tftp. Per Lumen Black Lotus Labs report Jun 2026.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html
  - https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_arch:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'mipsel64'
      - 'mipsel'
      - 'mips64'
  selection_download:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'wget'
      - 'curl'
      - 'tftp'
      - 'ftpget'
  condition: selection_arch and selection_download
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*mipsel64* OR *mipsel* OR *mips64*) @process.command_line:(*wget* OR *curl* OR *tftp* OR *ftpget*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| #event_platform=Lin
| regex("(mipsel64|mipsel|mips64|\\smips\\s)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(wget|curl|tftp|ftpget|busybox\\s+wget)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","ash","busybox") AND (Processes.process="*uname*" OR Processes.process="*/proc/cpuinfo*") AND (Processes.process="*mips*" OR Processes.process="*mipsel*" OR Processes.process="*mips64*") by Processes.dest Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","ash","busybox") AND (Processes.process="*uname*" OR Processes.process="*/proc/cpuinfo*") AND (Processes.process="*mips*" OR Processes.process="*mipsel*" OR Processes.process="*mips64*") by Processes.dest Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | sort - firstTime
Coordinated periodic beaconing fanout across many internal devices AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2 signature implied by a 1,500-device botnet: many internal hosts beaconing to a small set of public destinations on a near-regular interval with low byte volume per connection. The detection finds the destination-side cluster (multiple distinct internal sources, narrow time-interval distribution). Rationale: Article: '1,500 compromised devices' (up from 650) report 'structured reconnaissance data' to 'central servers' — implies a converging C2 fanout from many compromised devices into a small number of dispatch servers. Detection looks for the convergent pattern at the destination side (the C2 IP receives connections from many distinct internal sources). Sigma omitted — this is a count/threshold aggregation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SaaS endpoint (Windows Update, Slack, Microsoft Graph) hit by every workstation
  • CDN edge IP that fronts many domains (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly)
  • Internal proxy or DNS forwarder making outbound on behalf of every host (apparent fanout)
  • Time-synchronisation server NTP traffic
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in (dynamic(["8.8.8.8","1.1.1.1","168.63.129.16"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: reverse-DNS the destination IP and ASN-lookup; check against Microsoft / AWS / Google CDN ranges; reference Tor relay list (UC1) and threat-intel feeds; if it's a major SaaS, suppress and refine. Step 2 — Contain: if destination is unknown / VPS / consumer-ISP, block at perimeter and alert on any retry; preserve PCAP of next 10 minutes of traffic to that IP for jitter/pattern analysis. Step 3 — Hunt: query the source IP set — what device class are they? If SOHO/IoT-class fanout, cross-reference UC2 for the same set to confirm scanning activity; pivot the C2 IP for any other ports it serves; check whether any of the source IPs are external (i.e. through an internet-facing JDY-infected device tunneling back in).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443, 53)
| summarize DistinctSources = dcount(DeviceId), TotalConns = count(), Sources = make_set(DeviceName, 50), MeanIntervalSec = avg(datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev(Timestamp))) by RemoteIP, RemotePort, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctSources >= 20
| summarize PeakFanout = max(DistinctSources), TotalSourceFanout = sum(DistinctSources), TotalConns = sum(TotalConns), Sources = make_set(Sources, 100) by RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where TotalSourceFanout >= 50
| order by TotalSourceFanout desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventResult =~ "Success"
| where NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound"
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8080, 8443, 53)
| summarize DistinctSources = dcount(SrcIpAddr), TotalConns = count(), Sources = make_set(SrcHostname, 50) by DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctSources >= 20
| summarize PeakFanout = max(DistinctSources), TotalSourceFanout = sum(DistinctSources), TotalConns = sum(TotalConns), Sources = make_set(Sources, 100) by DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where TotalSourceFanout >= 50
| order by TotalSourceFanout desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Initiated:true -@DestinationIp:(10.* OR 172.16.* OR 172.17.* OR 172.18.* OR 172.19.* OR 172.20.* OR 172.21.* OR 172.22.* OR 172.23.* OR 172.24.* OR 172.25.* OR 172.26.* OR 172.27.* OR 172.28.* OR 172.29.* OR 172.30.* OR 172.31.* OR 192.168.*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ConnectionDirection=1
| RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=8080 OR RemotePort=8443 OR RemotePort=53
| groupBy([RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, bucket(span=1h)], function={ DistinctSources := count(field=aid, distinct=true) | Total := count() })
| DistinctSources >= 20
| groupBy([RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function={ PeakFanout := max(DistinctSources) | TotalConns := sum(Total) })
| PeakFanout >= 20

Mass internal-recon command bursts across multiple hosts AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the article's stated objective ('discover, fingerprint, and continuously map exposed services at scale') translated to on-host indicators: bursts of native discovery commands (net view, net user, net group, ipconfig, arp, systeminfo, nbtstat) executed across many hosts in a short window — the post-foothold reconnaissance phase that JDY-class operators run after exploitation. Rationale: Article frames JDY as an 'industrialized reconnaissance effort' for 'follow-on target identification and exploitation.' On any Windows estate breached as part of the same campaign, the post-foothold step is mass recce — the article's language ('discover, fingerprint, continuously map') maps to standard discovery TTPs. Threshold (>=10 distinct hosts per user per hour) tuned to the article's claim of scale. Sigma omitted — count/threshold across hosts is not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018/
ATT&CKT1087 T1018 T1016 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Domain admin running scheduled inventory script across the estate
  • SCCM / Tanium / Lansweeper agent issuing native commands as part of inventory collection
  • IT helpdesk training session walking through troubleshooting commands
  • Vulnerability assessment tool with credentialed scanning against many hosts
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("sccm-svc","tanium-svc","lansweeper-svc","helpdesk-admin")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the AccountName — is it an admin, service account, or standard user? Pull the same user's 7-day baseline for these binaries; if first-time observed, escalate. Cross-reference with concurrent network-scanning alerts from UC2. Step 2 — Contain: revoke the user's active Kerberos tickets and force password reset; isolate the originating jumpbox if pivoting through one. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the user's sessions across DeviceLogonEvents looking for the source RemoteIP — is it internal (lateral) or external (suspect direct compromise)? Sweep DeviceProcessEvents for any of the destination hosts running shell-dropper artifacts from UC3.
let RecceBinaries = dynamic(["net.exe","net1.exe","ipconfig.exe","arp.exe","systeminfo.exe","nbtstat.exe","nltest.exe","dsquery.exe","whoami.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where FileName in~ (RecceBinaries)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
| summarize Hosts = dcount(DeviceId), HostNames = make_set(DeviceName, 30), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 50), TotalExecs = count() by AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Hosts >= 10
| order by Hosts desc
let RecceBinaries = dynamic(["net.exe","net1.exe","ipconfig.exe","arp.exe","systeminfo.exe","nbtstat.exe","nltest.exe","dsquery.exe","whoami.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ExecName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ExecName in~ (RecceBinaries)
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("SYSTEM","LOCAL SERVICE","NETWORK SERVICE")
| summarize Hosts = dcount(Computer), HostNames = make_set(Computer, 30), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine, 50), TotalExecs = count() by SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Hosts >= 10
| order by Hosts desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\net.exe OR *\net1.exe OR *\ipconfig.exe OR *\arp.exe OR *\systeminfo.exe OR *\nbtstat.exe OR *\nltest.exe OR *\dsquery.exe OR *\NET.EXE OR *\IPCONFIG.EXE) -@SubjectUserName:*$
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("\\\\(net|net1|ipconfig|arp|systeminfo|nbtstat|nltest|dsquery|whoami)\\.exe$", field=ImageFileName, flags=i)
| NOT UserName=/\$$/
| groupBy([UserName, bucket(span=1h)], function={ DistinctHosts := count(field=aid, distinct=true) | TotalExecs := count() })
| DistinctHosts >= 10
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as cmdlines from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","ipconfig.exe","arp.exe","systeminfo.exe","nbtstat.exe","nltest.exe","dsquery.exe") AND Processes.user!="*$" by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | stats dc(dest) as DistinctHosts values(dest) as Hosts sum(count) as TotalCmds by user _time | where DistinctHosts >= 10 | sort - DistinctHosts
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmdlines from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","ipconfig.exe","arp.exe","systeminfo.exe","nbtstat.exe","nltest.exe","dsquery.exe") AND Processes.user!="*$" by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | stats dc(dest) as DistinctHosts values(dest) as Hosts sum(count) as TotalCmds by user _time | where DistinctHosts >= 10 | sort - DistinctHosts
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

SecurityEvent

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 pre-auth RCE via handleMessage endpoint AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage endpoint that watchTowr Labs identified as the exploit path for CVE-2026-10520 (CVSS 10.0). The patch redirects unauthenticated requests to a login page, so any unauthenticated success-shaped hit against this URI after patching is malicious. Hunting pre-patch hits also surfaces in-the-wild probing. Rationale: The /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage URI is the exact path watchTowr Labs disclosed as the CVE-2026-10520 exploitation route (quoted directly in the article). Any unauthenticated HTTP hit to this endpoint maps 1:1 to the published exploit; the article also notes the patch added an auth layer in front of it, so post-patch hits should never succeed unauthenticated.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7, Nuclei templates) probing for CVE-2026-10520 after disclosure
  • Red-team / penetration-test engagements scoped against Sentry
  • Ivanti support diagnostic scripts that legitimately call /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config endpoints from an authenticated admin session
  • Pre-disclosure baseline traffic from internal MDM operators (rare but possible since the endpoint exists pre-patch)
  • Health-check probes from upstream load balancers if the Sentry healthcheck path overlaps
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Qualys" and RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei" and RequestClientApplication !has "Rapid7"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on SourceIP and DestinationHostName. Pull the full request (RequestMethod, body length, response code) and any subsequent requests within 30s — successful exploitation typically chains into a command-execution payload. Check whether the source IP belongs to a sanctioned scanner via ASN/asset lookup. 2) Contain: if the source is external or unsanctioned, block at the perimeter (WAF rule on the URI prefix) and isolate the Sentry appliance from production network. Snapshot the appliance for forensics before reboot/patch. 3) Hunt: search the same SourceIP across all other Ivanti/MDM URIs for reconnaissance, look for outbound connections from the Sentry appliance IP (egress shell), and audit Sentry admin accounts created in the prior 30 days for CVE-2026-10523 (auth-bypass admin creation) co-occurrence.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
   or RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let SentryEndpoint = "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage";
let WAFHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has SentryEndpoint
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction;
let IISHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage" or csUriStem has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/"
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP = cIP, DestinationIP = Computer, DestinationHostName = sSiteName, RequestURL = strcat(csUriStem, iff(isnotempty(csUriQuery), strcat("?", csUriQuery), "")), RequestMethod = csMethod, RequestClientApplication = csUserAgent, DeviceVendor = "Microsoft", DeviceProduct = "IIS", DeviceAction = tostring(scStatus);
let ASIMHits = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has SentryEndpoint
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP = SrcIpAddr, DestinationIP = DstIpAddr, DestinationHostName = DstHostname, RequestURL = Url, RequestMethod = HttpMethod, RequestClientApplication = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DeviceVendor = EventVendor, DeviceProduct = EventProduct, DeviceAction = tostring(HttpStatusCode);
union WAFHits, IISHits, ASIMHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
